sources.label: MDPM 826 Usability Test Report — Team Zig
sources.detail: Moderated remote formative study. 6 participants, 31 Part 1 task attempts: 25 passes, 5 completions after a hint, 1 failure. 13 issues rated Critical, Major or Minor.

sources.label: Blue Rewards Ecosystem and Complexity Analysis v1.0
sources.detail: Independent research synthesis. Six complexity dimensions, four clocks, findings F01 to F13, and a program-state versus experienced-state comparison.

sources.label: Requirements Specification (MDPM 883), in the PRD
sources.detail: 37 functional requirements and the non-functional set across look and feel, usability, performance and security.

sources.label: Blue Rewards Data Pipeline (MDPM 830)
sources.detail: Generate, Collect, Keep and Shape, Store, Use. Three pilot measures: Opportunity Capture Rate, Earned Value Realization Rate, End-to-End Realization Rate.

findings.issue: A participant believed a missing-points inquiry had been submitted when it had not.
findings.systemReading: The member acted, the system did not register the act, and nothing told either party they disagreed. On the map this is a broken return leg: the member's action never becomes recorded activity, so no correction can start.

findings.issue: Participants looked for a dedicated Reward Goals tab before finding the placemat on Home.
findings.systemReading: A capability the member cannot locate does not reach them, which is the same failure as an opportunity no channel carries. The feature existed; the channel did not surface it where they looked.

findings.issue: A participant overlooked the comparison controls at the bottom of the screen.
findings.systemReading: Friction stalling the assessment before it starts. The member had the options in front of them and could not begin weighing them.

findings.issue: A participant struggled to locate the overdue-points alert on Home.
findings.systemReading: The system knew value was overdue and the member did not. Recorded position and member awareness diverged with no prompt to close the gap.

findings.issue: Back navigation sometimes returned a participant to an unexpected screen.
findings.systemReading: The clearest evidence that interface friction is a condition across the whole progression rather than a property of one stage.

findings.issue: A participant read the passed posting date as meaning the overdue points could no longer be used.
findings.systemReading: Two different clocks collapsed into one. Posting time says when points are credited; expiry says when they stop being spendable. The member treated a delay as a loss.

findings.issue: The label Points to use left members unsure whether the amount was points required, spent or remaining.
findings.systemReading: One label spanning three different value states. The map separates Potential, Earned, Available and Realized precisely because they are different things; the interface did not.

findings.issue: Comparison showed cash-purchase and points-redemption options together in different formats.
findings.systemReading: Earning and spending are opposite directions through the chain. Presenting them in one list asks the member to hold both directions at once.

findings.issue: Ask Blue accepted a goal to save toward a car, then asked pickup and drop-off questions. The participant abandoned the chat.
findings.systemReading: The filter failed to bound itself to the catalogue. Decisioning surfaced something that is not an opportunity in this system, which is the one job that arrow has.

findings.issue: A participant could not tell how projected earnings contributed toward the points still needed.
findings.systemReading: Points already held and points expected to arrive sit in different states. Shown as one number, the member cannot tell what is theirs now.

findings.issue: A participant was unsure whether their existing 30,000 points counted toward the goal target.
findings.systemReading: Direct evidence for the entry question the map already carries: a member joins the cycle wherever their balance puts them, and the product did not say so.

findings.issue: A participant was unsure whether Ask Blue's results would appear in chat or elsewhere on the page.
findings.systemReading: The member could not tell whether the system had acted. Status is not a cosmetic concern here; it determines whether they try again or stop.

findings.issue: A participant questioned why they would use Reward Goals at all. Another said it would not change their decisions.
findings.systemReading: The return leg of the flywheel, tested and not confirmed. If realized value does not change what the member does next, the loop does not compound and the engine the whole team drew does not start.

findings.issue: Changes to the balance after a resolution were difficult to identify and verify.
findings.systemReading: Value arrived and was not noticed. Unobserved value cannot feed back, so a correct outcome produces no engagement.

stageCounts.note: Counted by the value stage each issue acts on. Seven of the fourteen sit at Potential Value, the stage where the member works out what something is worth. None sit at Opportunity, which is the programme's side of the chain and was never in front of a participant.

rows.gloss: The catalogue. Not tested, and not visible to a member.
Working out what it is worth. Every severity band appears here.
The posting gap, read as expiry.
Knowing what is overdue and what is already spendable.

rows.stage: Realized Value and the return leg
rows.gloss: Whether value arrived, and whether it changed anything.
Navigation. Confirms friction is a condition, not a stage.

requirementClusters.heading: Make the catalogue reachable
requirementClusters.acts: Data and decisioning → Potential Value, Partner ecosystem → Opportunity
requirementClusters.loop: TR1 relevance flywheel · TR3 partner coverage
requirementClusters.reading: These are the filter. They decide what a member ever sees, which is the one thing that moves value out of Opportunity. FR8 and FR9 are the balancing condition made explicit: the catalogue still has to work when no external data is connected. FR8a and FR8b are the offer clock — stop showing what the member can no longer act on.

requirementClusters.heading: Make it judgeable
requirementClusters.acts: Channels and delivery → Potential Value, Interface friction → Potential Value
requirementClusters.reading: The largest cluster, acting on the stage where seven of the fourteen tested issues landed. FR24, the monetary equivalent and the basis of the estimate, answers the single most repeated complaint in the study.

requirementClusters.heading: Make qualifying legible
requirementClusters.acts: Products and transactions → Earned Value, Service and operations → Earned Value
requirementClusters.reading: Qualification is where the member's act meets the programme's rules. The complexity analysis calls this eligibility time; these requirements make its state visible instead of inferred.

requirementClusters.heading: Separate earned from spendable
requirementClusters.acts: Service and operations → Available Value, Points balance → Available Value
requirementClusters.reading: FR23 splits the balance from unposted earnings, which is the gap the map draws between Earned Value and Available Value. FR25 and FR26 are the notifications that keep the two clocks apart — the distinction one participant got wrong.

requirementClusters.heading: Confirm value arrived
requirementClusters.reading: The smallest cluster, and the one the testing found least evidence for. Value that arrives unnoticed cannot feed the return leg.

requirementClusters.heading: Diagnose and recover loss
requirementClusters.acts: Available Value → Correction and recovery, Realized Value → Correction and recovery
requirementClusters.reading: Six requirements exist purely to find out why value did not arrive and to get it back. The September map had nowhere for them: it drew where value is lost but never the path back. That gap is what the Extension to the Map closes — Correction and recovery is now a node with seven connections, and these six requirements are what it does.

requirementClusters.heading: Keep permission with the member
requirementClusters.loop: TB2 trust and consent · permission brake
requirementClusters.reading: The permission brake, written as requirements. FR18 — approval before anything changes a balance, goal, redemption or data permission — is the brake itself, and the security set S1 to S7b holds it in place.

clocks.note: From the November complexity analysis. The five value stages implicitly assume value moves on a single timeline. It does not, and the gap between two of these clocks is already a Major usability issue.

rows.name: Eligibility time
rows.what: When the action must happen for the terms to be satisfied.

rows.name: Recognition time
rows.what: When evidence of the action reaches the service that can act on it.

rows.name: Posting time
rows.what: When points are actually credited to the balance.

rows.name: Realization time
rows.what: When the member receives value they can use.

clocks.consequence: A delay between recognition and posting is not a failure, but it looks exactly like one. One participant read a passed posting date as the points no longer being usable. Absence of points is not evidence that points are missing, and the product has to be able to say which of the four clocks it is waiting on.

gaps.lead: What the system records, and what the member believes
gaps.note: Adapted from the complexity analysis. Each row is a place where the programme can be entirely correct and the member still wrong. Marked where the usability study saw the same gap in a participant.

rows.believed: The member has not checked the balance
rows.evidence: “So even if my points go up by a bit, I will probably not notice.”

rows.believed: The member assumes the points are missing
rows.evidence: The whole missing-points flow, tasks 5 and 6.

rows.believed: The member cannot tell what changed
rows.evidence: “There’s no notification that says that I received the points.”

rows.believed: The member expects to earn automatically
rows.evidence: Not reached in this study. Activation was not one of the six tasks.

rows.believed: The member believes the exact product qualified
rows.evidence: Not tested. Receipt earning was outside the prototype.
Scenario 2 covered this, but Part 2 produced only four attempts.

rows.believed: The member thinks the net cost is available now
rows.evidence: Not tested. This is the November points-back promotion case.

gaps.closing: Three of the seven gaps were confirmed in front of participants. Four were not reached. That split is the argument for the next round of testing, and it is why the 90,000-point scenario matters: it is where redemption and fulfilment live.

whatChanged.claim: Members cannot tell what their points are worth.
whatChanged.why: The most repeated finding in the study, across offer comparison, goal setting and transaction review. Four participants asked for a conversion they could not find.

whatChanged.claim: Interface friction acts at every stage of the progression.
whatChanged.why: Fourteen issues spread across five stages, with back-navigation failing independently of any one of them.

The return leg five of six contributors drew is the one the testing did not confirm. Two participants said progress tracking would not change their decisions. This is a loop assumption, and it is now the weakest link in the engine.

whatChanged.claim: A member joins the cycle wherever their balance puts them.
whatChanged.why: A participant with 30,000 points could not tell whether those points counted toward their goal — the entry question, asked unprompted.

whatChanged.claim: Decisioning bounds what becomes a visible opportunity.
whatChanged.why: Ask Blue accepted a goal the catalogue cannot satisfy. The filter is the mechanism the product depends on and it did not hold.
